approved: Health and Other Services (Compensation) Care Charges (Amendment) Bill 2014
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record

This bill is part of a two-bill package that also includes the Aged Care and Other Legislation Amendment Bill 2014, together addressing a gap in recovering past care costs for home care when a care recipient gets compensation.
The package would align home care cost recovery with existing residential care rules, allowing the Commonwealth to recover such costs from compensation payments.
The amendments that expand charges on compensation are placed in this separate bill to satisfy section 55 of the Constitution.
The bill would amend the Health and Other Services (Compensation) Care Charges Act 1995 to enable recovery of past home care costs from compensation payments.
The bill would remove the inequality between home and residential care in cost recovery.
The bill would help avoid delays in moving to residential care while compensation is pending.
The bill would reduce financial losses to the Commonwealth.
Home care recipients who receive compensation payments, and the Commonwealth.

Supported most of the Aged Care and Other Legislation Amendment Bill 2014 including the 1 January 2015 rollout of the My Aged Care gateway, but sought to amend provisions removing Labor's aged-care workforce supplement, citing the 2010 Intergenerational report's finding that a 300 per cent increase in aged-care workers will be needed by the middle of the century.

Defended the government's changes to aged care funding, arguing that redirecting the $1.5 billion Aged Care Workforce Supplement back to providers was fairer than Labor's centrally planned scheme, and that the dementia supplement had blown out tenfold in cost, while highlighting that Tasmania has the largest and fastest growing aged population of any Australian state.

Supported the Aged Care and Other Legislation Amendment Bill, noting her electorate of Ryan has 13 nursing homes and care facilities, and criticised Labor's $1.5 billion Aged Care Workforce Supplement for only benefiting workers covered by an enterprise bargaining agreement, effectively pressuring them to join a union.

Opposed the redirection of Labor's $1.2 billion aged-care workforce supplement, which had aimed to lift pay for around 350,000 workers, disputing government claims it was tied to union membership, and cited the Productivity Commission's prediction that Australia will need three times its existing aged-care workforce by 2050, noting a 2011 census finding that 49 per cent of aged-care registered nurses were aged 50 or older.

Supported amendments to the aged-care bills requiring that the $1.1 billion being redirected to providers under this legislation actually be spent on workforce pay and conditions, criticising the government's June 2014 decision to abandon both the $653 million Aged Care Payroll Tax Supplement and the Dementia and Severe Behaviours Supplement without guaranteeing the funds would benefit workers.

Argued against the Aged Care and Other Legislation Amendment Bill, saying it would abolish the $1.1 billion aged care workforce supplement and dump the $16.15 a day dementia supplement introduced by Labor, warning this would leave aged care residents worse off as staffing levels struggle to keep pace with an ageing population.

Argued in support of the Aged Care and Other Legislation Amendment Bill and the Health and Other Services (Compensation) Care Charges (Amendment) Bill, saying they would support stage 2 of the aged care gateway and online portal and allow recovery of past home care costs where a care recipient receives a compensation payment.
